ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants completed the 45-item version of Sternberg's Triangular Love Scale and reported their age, gender, relationship length, and economic situation.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .056", "p = .843", "p = .146", "p = .298", "p = .453", "p = .373", "p = .162"), Sentence = c("In these films the fall is weaker than the rise: the slope in 2020 is -0.011 points per year in M4 (t(49) = -1.95, p = .056) and -0.016 in M3 (t(49) = -2.99, p = .004).", "The interaction of PI with squared HDI, added to M1, was close to zero (b = 0.002, p = .843).", "First, across countries, extreme responding was not associated with HDI, whether measured by the share of answers at the top of the scale (r = 0.22, p = .146) or with a multi-process item response model (r = 0.16, p = .298; Böckenholt & Meiser, 2017).", "First, across countries, extreme responding was not associated with HDI, whether measured by the share of answers at the top of the scale (r = 0.22, p = .146) or with a multi-process item response model (r = 0.16, p = .298; Böckenholt & Meiser, 2017).", "Trust predicted the idealization slope when it replaced HDI in M1 (b = -0.030, p = .013), but not when both entered the model (b = -0.009, p = .453), whereas HDI remained (b = -0.046, p = .004).", "Weighted by the number of respondents, the association was close to zero (r = -0.07, p = .373), with the five largest samples carrying 31% of the weight.", "It was clear among men (β = -0.23, z = -4.97, p < .001) but not among women (β = -0.06, z = -1.40, p = .162; Supplementary Note 5)." )), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 23 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 17 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

table <- structure(list(Order = 1:17, File = c("study1_functions.R", "study1_analysis.R", 
"study1_robustness.R", "study1_romance_tag.R", "nomance_study3.R", 
"Study 3/Scripts/study3_functions.R", "study3_analysis.R", "Study 3/With 38 countries/study3_functions.R", 
"study3_irtree.R", "study3_robustness.R", "study3_figure3.R", 
"study3_submitted.R", "study4_functions.R", "study4_analysis.R", 
"analysis_study4.R", "study4_robustness.R", "love_analysis.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "study1_functions.R", "study1_functions.R", 
"study1_functions.R", "—", "—", "Study 3/Scripts/study3_functions.R", 
"—", "Study 3/Scripts/study3_functions.R", "Study 3/Scripts/study3_functions.R", 
"study3_analysis.R, study3_robustness.R", "Study 3/With 38 countries/study3_functions.R", 
"—", "study4_functions.R", "study4_analysis.R", "study4_functions.R", 
"—"), Basis = c("numeric", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", 
"numeric", "numeric", "dependency", "numeric", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "numeric", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -17L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `study1_functions.R` to `Scripts/study1_functions.R` (in study1_robustness.R); `data/context/human-development-index.csv` to `../Study 4/Old version - First submission/human-development-index.csv` (in study1_robustness.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **8 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files not run on their own
2 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 10 scripts: 0 ran without error, 5 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 4 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **7 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded**: study1_analysis.R, study1_robustness.R, study1_romance_tag.R, study4_analysis.R, analysis_study4.R, study4_robustness.R, love_analysis.R. They are not counted as scripts that did not reproduce. The files: Study 1/Data/MOVIES_LOVE_MERGED.csv (158.9 MB), Study 4/Data/Final_dataset.csv (125.4 MB), Study 4/Old version - First submission/Final_dataset.csv (125.4 MB), Study 1/Old version - First submission/MOVIES_LOVE_MERGED.csv (158.9 MB); files over 100 MB are not downloaded. **2 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `study3_irtree.R` (love_database.csv); `study3_robustness.R` (love_database.csv). Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **2 scripts looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `Study 3/Data/love_database.csv` to `Study 3/Scripts/data/love_database.csv` for `study3_analysis.R`; `Study 3/Data/love_database.csv` to `Study 3/data/love_database.csv` for `study3_submitted.R`; `Study 3/Data/HDI.csv` to `Study 3/Scripts/data/HDI.csv` for `study3_analysis.R`; `Study 3/Data/HDI.csv` to `Study 3/data/HDI.csv` for `study3_submitted.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
**Calls that install packages in the code**

3 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.
**Run by another script**

4 scripts are run by another script with `source()`, so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

text.text: Converging evidence shows that the cultural importance of romantic love has increased with societal development: it guides the choice of partners, founds families, and pervades cultural production.

In a survey of 9,474 participants across 45 countries, reports of romantic love peak and then decline at the highest levels of development, and romantic content in 13,415 U.S. movies rose and then fell between 1971 and 2020.
This poses a puzzle: if romantic love sustains long-term pair-bonds, and if safer, more affluent environments make such bonds more viable, why would love decline where it should thrive?
We propose that what declines is not love, but the need to signal it.

A formal model shows that when long-term commitment becomes common, overt romantic signaling becomes unnecessary and even counterproductive: the most committed individuals benefit from not signaling, because doing so would reveal that they expected the relationship to need reassurance.

Consistent with this account, in cross-national data (N = 8,792 and 84,382), idealizing items of a love scale are endorsed less, relative to other items, and reported infidelity is lower in more developed countries.
In affluent societies, love becomes quieter not because bonds are weaker, but because they are more secure.
From a functional perspective, romantic love is commonly understood as a psychological mechanism that helps sustain long-term pair-bonding and cooperative parenting (Fletcher et al., 2015).
text.formatted: From a functional perspective, romantic love is commonly understood as a psychological mechanism that helps sustain long-term pair-bonding and cooperative parenting <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fletcher et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Attachment to a particular partner can motivate individuals to invest in the relationship and maintain it through difficulties, allowing cooperation to extend beyond immediate exchanges.

Such lasting bonds can facilitate the sharing of resources and caregiving responsibilities, increasing the likelihood that offspring receive sustained care and investment (Quinlan, 2007; Kowal et al., 2024; Conroy-Beam et al., 2015; Walter et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Such lasting bonds can facilitate the sharing of resources and caregiving responsibilities, increasing the likelihood that offspring receive sustained care and investment <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Quinlan, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Kowal et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Conroy-Beam et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Walter et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: From this functional perspective, societal development should create conditions favorable to romantic love.
Investments in a lasting relationship, such as building a shared household, supporting a partner, and raising children together, yield many of their benefits over time.
Their expected returns therefore depend partly on whether people can afford these investments and expect to benefit from them in the future.

When immediate material needs are pressing and the future is uncertain, allocating resources to distant benefits is perceived as less worthwhile (Boon-Falleur et al., 2025; Mell et al., 2021; Pepper & Nettle, 2017).
text.formatted: When immediate material needs are pressing and the future is uncertain, allocating resources to distant benefits is perceived as less worthwhile <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Boon-Falleur et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Mell et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Pepper & Nettle, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Because greater material security can ease these constraints, it is associated with longer time horizons (Bulley & Pepper, 2017; Griskevicius et al., 2011; Sunde et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Because greater material security can ease these constraints, it is associated with longer time horizons <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bulley & Pepper, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Griskevicius et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Sunde et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To the extent that societal development makes sustained cooperation between partners more feasible and rewarding, it should favor the motivations that support such relationships, including romantic love (Li & Zheng, 2021; see Boon-Falleur et al., 2025).
text.formatted: To the extent that societal development makes sustained cooperation between partners more feasible and rewarding, it should favor the motivations that support such relationships, including romantic love <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Li & Zheng, 2021</ref>; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Boon-Falleur et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, couples facing economic hardship report more conflict and separate more often (Conger et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, couples facing economic hardship report more conflict and separate more often <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Conger et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This account provides a basis for asking how romantic love, and its different manifestations, vary with the social and material conditions that favor lasting relationships.
Yet, addressing it across societies and historical periods requires measures that capture its manifestations beyond directly observed interactions between partners.
The solution lies in the fact that romantic love extends beyond the private experience of being in love.
It is expressed in how people answer questionnaires and in the stories they seek out and enjoy.

These aspects of romantic life are related: nonverbal displays of love covary with self-reported love and with partners' perceptions of love (Gonzaga et al., 2001), and expressiveness has been linked to both affectionate behavior and partner idealization (Miller et al., 2003).
text.formatted: These aspects of romantic life are related: nonverbal displays of love covary with self-reported love and with partners' perceptions of love <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gonzaga et al., 2001)</ref>, and expressiveness has been linked to both affectionate behavior and partner idealization <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Miller et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Interest in fictional romances is also positively associated with idealized beliefs about romantic love (van Monsjou & Mar, 2019).
text.formatted: Interest in fictional romances is also positively associated with idealized beliefs about romantic love <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(van Monsjou & Mar, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Coming back to variations of romantic love with ecological conditions, evidence from literary history, quantitative text analysis and econometric methods show that societal development is associated with and may causally increase references to romantic love over historical time (Baumard et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Coming back to variations of romantic love with ecological conditions, evidence from literary history, quantitative text analysis and econometric methods show that societal development is associated with and may causally increase references to romantic love over historical time <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baumard et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern holds across European and non-European cultures alike, including the Arab world, Persia, India, China and Japan (Baumard et al., 2022;  for correlational studies, see : Zhong et al., 2023 : Zhong et al., , 2025;; Samani et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This pattern holds across European and non-European cultures alike, including the Arab world, Persia, India, China and Japan <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baumard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for correlational studies, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">: Zhong et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">: Zhong et al., , 2025;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Samani et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Synchronic evidence points in the same direction: a cross-cultural survey of 9,474 participants across 45 countries reports higher levels of intimacy, passion, and commitment in societies with higher Human Development Index (HDI) (Sorokowski et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Synchronic evidence points in the same direction: a cross-cultural survey of 9,474 participants across 45 countries reports higher levels of intimacy, passion, and commitment in societies with higher Human Development Index (HDI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Sorokowski et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Together, historical analyses and contemporary cross-cultural surveys converge on the same conclusion: romantic love increases as societies become more secure.
Yet this relationship may not continue indefinitely.

In the same survey, the overall love score, passion and commitment peak and then decline above an HDI of about 0.85, but intimacy does not (Sorokowski et al., 2023; on the role of response styles, see Ulitzsch et al., 2024, and Sorokowski & Kowal, 2024).
text.formatted: In the same survey, the overall love score, passion and commitment peak and then decline above an HDI of about 0.85, but intimacy does not <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Sorokowski et al., 2023</ref>; on the role of response styles, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Ulitzsch et al., 2024, and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Sorokowski &</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Kowal, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This quantitative trend is consistent with qualitative observations, mostly from educated, affluent groups, that overt romantic demonstrations can produce discomfort rather than admiration. Eco (1983 Eco ( /1984) ) described the predicament of a man who cannot tell an educated woman 'I love you madly', because both know the phrase has already been written by a popular romance novelist; he can only say it by quoting it.
text.formatted: This quantitative trend is consistent with qualitative observations, mostly from educated, affluent groups, that overt romantic demonstrations can produce discomfort rather than admiration. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Eco (1983</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Eco ( /1984) )</ref> described the predicament of a man who cannot tell an educated woman 'I love you madly', because both know the phrase has already been written by a popular romance novelist; he can only say it by quoting it.

text.text: In interviews, uppermiddle-class Americans express ironic distance from romantic clichés more readily than workingclass respondents (Illouz, 1997), and treat 'mythic' love as naïve (Swidler, 2001).
text.formatted: In interviews, uppermiddle-class Americans express ironic distance from romantic clichés more readily than workingclass respondents <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Illouz, 1997)</ref>, and treat 'mythic' love as naïve <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Swidler, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The vocabulary itself is recent: in the Google Books corpus of English, expressions such as 'cheesy love', 'cheesy romance' and 'cheesy gesture' are practically absent before the 1990s and become more frequent after 2000 (our own use of Ngram in October 2026; see Michel et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The vocabulary itself is recent: in the Google Books corpus of English, expressions such as 'cheesy love', 'cheesy romance' and 'cheesy gesture' are practically absent before the 1990s and become more frequent after 2000 (our own use of Ngram in October 2026; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Michel et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Other indications concern the expression of romance rather than love itself: love themes became less frequent in U.S. top-40 lyrics after the 1970s (Madanikia & Bartholomew, 2014).
text.formatted: Other indications concern the expression of romance rather than love itself: love themes became less frequent in U.S. top-40 lyrics after the 1970s <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Madanikia & Bartholomew, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This poses a puzzle for functional accounts of love.

If romantic love is a mechanism designed to sustain long-term pair-bonds, and if safer, more affluent environments make such bonds more viable, why would love decline in the very societies where it should thrive?
To understand this paradox, it is first important to distinguish commitment to a relationship from the idealized representations that can accompany it.

Research on personal life and everyday intimacy cautions against equating changes in romantic ideals with a weakening of relationships. Smart (2007) emphasizes the enduring importance of connectedness, memory, and shared histories.
text.formatted: Research on personal life and everyday intimacy cautions against equating changes in romantic ideals with a weakening of relationships. <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Smart (2007)</ref> emphasizes the enduring importance of connectedness, memory, and shared histories.

text.text: Studies of couple relationships likewise highlight the importance of practical support, attentiveness, and small gestures of affection in sustaining intimacy (Jamieson, 1999; Gabb & Fink, 2015).
text.formatted: Studies of couple relationships likewise highlight the importance of practical support, attentiveness, and small gestures of affection in sustaining intimacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Jamieson, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Gabb & Fink, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these contributions motivate a distinction between idealized representations of romance and the everyday practices through which relationships are maintained.
They do not yet establish a historical shift from one to the other, but help explain why a decline in romantic idealization need not imply a corresponding decline in care or commitment.

We use "love" for the attachment that sustains long-term pair-bonds, and "romantic love" in a narrower sense than the functional literature cited above: the motivation to idealize the partner and to express this idealization overtly.
"Romantic signals" are these overt expressions, such as declarations, grand gestures and idealizing statements that present the partner or the relationship as exceptional.
Romantic love and romantic signals therefore vary together.
Their absence does not imply an absence of love, which can be expressed through the everyday practices described above.
Our account concerns the decline of romantic love and romantic signals, not of longterm love.
We therefore propose that what has changed is the adaptive value of romantic signals only.
Expressions of romantic love signal commitment, but they also reveal something about the sender's expectations: specifically, how much reassurance they believe the relationship requires.

In environments where trust is uncertain and long-term commitment cannot be taken for granted, overt romantic signals serve a clear function: they reduce doubt, align expectations, and stabilize cooperation.
Consistent with this, people make their relationship more visible on social media on days when they feel less secure about their partner's feelings (Emery et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, people make their relationship more visible on social media on days when they feel less secure about their partner's feelings <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Emery et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, in high-trust environments where commitment is increasingly presumed rather than negotiated, the same signals can acquire a different meaning.
Rather than reassuring, they may imply that the sender believes reassurance is still necessary, that the relationship is fragile, uncertain, or insufficiently secure.
Under these conditions, romantic signaling could become counterproductive.

When individuals anticipate the possibility of deep, low-maintenance cooperation (i.e., relationships that operate without constant reassurance) overt signals may force a reclassification of the relationship into a lower-trust mode, with shorter-term benefits.
This reclassification carries an opportunity cost: what appeared to be a high-trust, high-cooperation relationship is downgraded to one requiring explicit proof and more direct reciprocation.
The signal becomes aversive not because it indicates low commitment, but because it eliminates the possibility of an even more secure, longterm, effortless bond.
In this paper, we formalize this intuition and test some of its empirical implications.
We first show that romantic content in U.S. films rose and then fell between 1971 and 2020.
We then present a model of cooperative signaling in which a romantic signal conveys commitment but also reveals how much reassurance the sender expects the relationship to need.
The model predicts that overt signaling can become unnecessary, and even aversive, when long-term commitment is common.
Finally, we turn to cross-national survey data.

In more developed countries, respondents endorse items describing partner idealization less, relative to the other items of a love scale, and are slightly less likely to report having ever been unfaithful to a partner.

Together, these findings are consistent with the possibility that romantic signals become less prominent in affluent societies because commitment needs less demonstration, not because it has weakened.
Cross-sectional comparisons cannot distinguish historical change from stable differences between countries.
We therefore examined romantic content in U.S. films using a pre-registered diachronic analysis.
This tests whether cultural production shows a temporal pattern corresponding to the cross-national pattern reported by Sorokowski et al. (2023).
text.formatted: This tests whether cultural production shows a temporal pattern corresponding to the cross-national pattern reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Sorokowski et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: Cultural artifacts record the themes made available to audiences, making their content a good proxy of audience preferences (Baumard et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Cultural artifacts record the themes made available to audiences, making their content a good proxy of audience preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baumard et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For romance specifically, interest in fictional relationships is positively associated with idealizing romantic beliefs (van Monsjou & Mar, 2019), providing a link between cultural preferences and private romantic feelings.
text.formatted: For romance specifically, interest in fictional relationships is positively associated with idealizing romantic beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(van Monsjou & Mar, 2019)</ref>, providing a link between cultural preferences and private romantic feelings.

text.text: Narrative films provide a corpus in which romantic relationships vary in presence and centrality.
We use this variation to examine changes in the cultural prominence of romantic love across release years.
Our corpus comprises 13,415 U.S. feature films released between 1971 and 2020.
We obtained annotations using a pre-registered large language model protocol (see Methods; Dubourg et al., 2024; Rathje et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We obtained annotations using a pre-registered large language model protocol (see Methods; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Dubourg et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Rathje et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The primary Romantic Love Score rates "the significance of romantic love" on a 0-10 scale from the film title alone.
The prompt defines romantic love as "an allconsuming type of love, which is unconditional and enduring, capable of overcoming challenges and standing the test of time".
A broader General Love Score uses a different definition of love and serves as a replication.
Valid scores were available for 12,369 and 12,505 films, respectively.
Romantic Love scores (our main outcome variable) were missing for 1,046 films (7.8%).

A keyword search of the model's answers suggests that most noted that several films share the title (59%); others said the model did not know the film (18%), described little or no love story without giving a score (15%), or gave another answer without a score (8%).

Films without a score were older on average (mean release year 1998.2 vs 2000.2; Welch t(1233.5) = -4.71, p < .001): scores were missing for 10.1% of films released in [1971] [1972] [1973] [1974] [1975] [1976] [1977] [1978] [1979] 8.0% in the 1980s, 8.2% in the 1990s, 9.2% in the 2000s and 5.7% in 2010-2020.
text.formatted: Films without a score were older on average (mean release year 1998.2 vs 2000.2; Welch t(1233.5) = -4.71, p < .001): scores were missing for 10.1% of films released in <ref type="bibr">[1971]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1972]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1973]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1974]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1975]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1976]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1977]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1978]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[1979]</ref> <ref type="bibr">8</ref>.0% in the 1980s, 8.2% in the 1990s, 9.2% in the 2000s and 5.7% in 2010-2020.

text.text: Scores were missing for 17.8% of films in the fifth with the fewest IMDb votes, against 1.3% in the fifth with the most.
And they were also more often missing for films without the IMDb Romance tag (8.5%, against 4.3% for Romancetagged films).
Yearly means therefore do not cover quite the same types of films across periods, and the model knows some films better than others.
After the main results, we test whether this could produce the trend.

Romance-tagged films scored higher than other films, meeting the pre-registered criterion for proceeding with temporal analyses: M = 6.76 (SD = 2.53, n = 2,069) versus M = 2.80 (SD = 1.85, n = 10,300); Welch t(2532.0) = 67.63, p < .001; Cohen's d = 2.00, 95% CI [1.94, 2.05].
text.formatted: Romance-tagged films scored higher than other films, meeting the pre-registered criterion for proceeding with temporal analyses: M = 6.76 (SD = 2.53, n = 2,069) versus M = 2.80 (SD = 1.85, n = 10,300); Welch t(2532.0) = 67.63, p < .001; Cohen's d = 2.00, 95% CI [1.94, 2.05].

text.text: Because the IMDb tag is probably part of the model's training data, this comparison shows that the scores track the genre label, but it is not an independent assessment of film content.
We compared four pre-registered OLS models using AIC: linear and quadratic functions of release year, each with or without a production-volume control counting all corpus films released that year.
AIC values were 57,423.18 for M1 (linear), 57,412.00 for M2 (linear with control), 57,354.74 for M3 (quadratic), and 57,351.73 for M4 (quadratic with control).
M4 had the lowest AIC, 71.44 points below M1.
In M4, the squared-year term was negative: -0.198 points per SD of the predictor, 95% CI [-0.247, -0.149], t(12,365) = -7.90, p < .001.
text.formatted: In M4, the squared-year term was negative: -0.198 points per SD of the predictor, 95% CI [-0.247, -0.149], t(12,365) = -7.90, p < .001.

text.text: The linear year term was positive (0.168 per SD, p = .002).
The production control was small (-0.114, 95% CI [-0.214, -0.014], p = .025).
The squared-year term was similar without the control (M3: -0.208).
Because release year is the predictor, films released in the same year are not independent observations, and film-level standard errors overstate precision.

The squared-year term remained clearly different from zero with standard errors clustered on release year (t(49) = -7.37, p < .001) and when the model was fitted to the 50 yearly means, weighted by the number of films scored (t(46) = -6.65, p < .001).

To clarify the mechanism underlying the paradox described above, we introduce a formal model (detailed in Method and Supplementary Note 1).
The goal of the model is not to reproduce the full complexity of romantic relationships, but to isolate a minimal set of assumptions under which signals of commitment can become counterproductive.
The model captures two adaptive problems that arise in any relationship built on mutual cooperation.
First, individuals must attract and maintain trust, bearing the immediate costs of cooperation to build a reputation that sustains the relationship over time.
Second, they must decide whether to extend trust, predicting their partner's future behavior based on incomplete information.

In the model, these problems are separated into two roles: a signaler, who manages their reputation by deciding whether to reciprocate trust, and a chooser, who decides whether and how much to trust based on what they observe.
The signaler's willingness to reciprocate depends on their patience: how much they value future interactions relative to the immediate cost of cooperating.
More patient signalers reciprocate trust because the long-term benefits of maintaining trust outweigh the shortterm savings from cheating.

The chooser's challenge is to identify such partners, using the information available to them: the signaler's past reciprocation behavior, their signaling decisions, and the chooser's prior beliefs about the kind of partner they are likely to encounter.
Cooperation can occur at two levels.
The high level is more rewarding for both partners when it succeeds, but harder to sustain, requiring more patience from the signaler and more favorable beliefs from the chooser.

Signalers belong to one of three types, reflecting different levels of patience and reciprocation: low-patience types always cheat, mediumpatience types reciprocate trust only at the low level, and high-patience types always reciprocate.
Choosers are either high-trust or low-trust.

This distinction arises entirely from assortative matching: patient signalers are more likely to be paired with high-trust choosers, so that high-trust choosers have reason to be more optimistic about the signaler's patience.
Before interaction, the signaler may choose to send a costly signal: a visible gesture that reveals information to the chooser but does not change the signaler's type.
After observing whether a signal was sent, the chooser permanently sets the level of cooperation and decides whether to extend trust.
We show that this model admits an equilibrium in which signaling is aversive to high-trust choosers, represented in Figure 2.
text.formatted: We show that this model admits an equilibrium in which signaling is aversive to high-trust choosers, represented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: A-B. In this equilibrium, only medium-patience signalers send the signal.
Choosers interpret the signal accordingly: a signaler who sends reveals that they can sustain only low-level cooperation, so both chooser types set the level at low and trust.
A signaler who does not send is ambiguous: they are either low or high patience.
Low-trust choosers, who tend to be matched with less patient signalers, resolve this ambiguity unfavorably and distrust entirely.
High-trust choosers resolve it favorably: they set the level at high and trust.
The signal is aversive to high-trust choosers because of what it reveals about the signaler's beliefs.
Sending the signal communicates an expectation that the partner needs reassurance-that the relationship is uncertain enough to require explicit demonstration.

By the model's matching assumption, this expectation is correlated with the signaler's own patience: patient signalers, who tend to be matched with high-trust choosers, expect their partner to extend high-level trust without reassurance, while less patient signalers expect the opposite.

From the high-trust chooser's side, this is why receiving a signal is bad news: they were predisposed to expect a patient partner, and the signal reveals instead one who is cooperative but only at a basic level-willing to sustain the relationship, but not to invest in it fully.

text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: C shows the parameter combinations for which the aversive signaling equilibrium exists.
The vertical axis varies the difficulty of cooperation: the cost-to-benefit ratio of high-level reciprocation and high-level trust.
The horizontal axis captures population patience, by varying a single parameter that determines both the prevalence of patient signalers and of high-trust choosers.
As population patience increases, the equilibrium becomes sustainable across a wider range of cooperation difficulties.

This is primarily because higher patience makes it easier for high-trust choosers to justify extending highlevel trust to non-senders: the more patient the population, the more confident they can be that a non-sender is high-patience rather than low-patience.
At very high levels of population patience, however, the equilibrium disappears, because even low-trust choosers resolve the ambiguity of non-sending favorably and trust without needing a signal.
The model thus identifies conditions under which commitment signals become counterproductive.
Our analysis is static: we focus on the aversive signaling equilibrium, in which high-trust choosers respond unfavorably to signals, and derive the conditions under which it can be sustained.
Over the relevant range, increasing population patience expands its existence domain to include more difficult cooperation.
This motivates the expectation that more patient populations will more often exhibit aversive responses to signals, with highly committed individuals consequently signaling less.
The variables of the model are not directly observed in the data we analyze.
In the model, population patience determines how common long-term commitment is.
If socioeconomic development makes long-term commitment more common, as argued in the Introduction, it should make the aversive signaling equilibrium easier to sustain.
We therefore expect overt romantic signals to be received less favorably and sent less often in more developed societies.
The following studies test implications of this prediction with indirect measures.
Study 3 measures the endorsement of idealizing statements (i.e., an indirect measure of the motivation behind romantic signaling).
Study 4 measures selfreported infidelity (i.e., an indicator of how common long-term commitment is).
Neither study measures signals sent to a partner.
We use the Human Development Index as an indicator of the conditions that favor long-term commitment (not a direct measure of patience).

For the period covered by Study 1, behavioral indicators also suggest that time horizons lengthened in the United States: adolescents delayed dating, drinking and sexual activity (Twenge & Park, 2019), adult smoking declined (Jamal et al., 2016; Creamer et al., 2019), and the share of young adults with a college degree rose (National Center for Education Statistics, n.d.).

text.text: These trends were not uniform, as mortality from drug overdoses, suicide and alcohol rose among middle-aged white Americans, most of all among the less educated (Case & Deaton, 2015).

text.text: The formal model developed above predicts not a generalized decline in romantic motivation, but a selective decline in commitment signaling.
When long-term cooperation is uncertain, individuals benefit from emitting signals that reassure partners of their commitment.
However, once long-term commitment becomes sufficiently common in the population, these signals lose their function and even become counterproductive.

A critical empirical implication of this logic is that socio-economic development should selectively reduce expressions of love whose primary function is to signal commitment under uncertainty, while leaving intact (or even strengthening) other components of romantic relationships that directly sustain cooperation.
Testing this prediction raises a measurement problem.
A survey cannot observe signals sent to a partner: it records how respondents describe their feelings and their relationship.
What it can capture is the content that many romantic signals carry.

Overt expressions of love, such as declaring that the partner is unique or that nothing matters more than the relationship, often express partner idealization: they present the partner or the relationship as uniquely valuable, irreplaceable, or central to one's life.
Research on positive illusions treats idealization as a private appraisal that sustains relationship satisfaction (Murray et al., 1996 (Murray et al., , 2011)), not as a display.
text.formatted: Research on positive illusions treats idealization as a private appraisal that sustains relationship satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Murray et al., 1996</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Murray et al., , 2011))</ref>, not as a display.

text.text: Yet idealization has features that suggest a communicative function.

It departs systematically from accuracy: intimates see their partners more positively than the partners see themselves (Murray et al., 1996), and not every partner can be the most attractive or the most important person in the world.
text.formatted: It departs systematically from accuracy: intimates see their partners more positively than the partners see themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Murray et al., 1996)</ref>, and not every partner can be the most attractive or the most important person in the world.

text.text: Idealization also has the form that credible commitment takes.

Someone who does not weigh the relationship against its alternatives can be trusted more than someone who does (Frank, 1988; Hoffman et al., 2015), and idealizing statements such as "nothing is more important to me than my relationship" say precisely that.
text.formatted: Someone who does not weigh the relationship against its alternatives can be trusted more than someone who does <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Frank, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Hoffman et al., 2015)</ref>, and idealizing statements such as "nothing is more important to me than my relationship" say precisely that.

text.text: Finally, idealization reaches the partner: people are more satisfied when their partner idealizes them (Murray et al., 1996).
text.formatted: Finally, idealization reaches the partner: people are more satisfied when their partner idealizes them <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Murray et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Idealization is also tied to the expression of love, and expressions of love are read as commitment.

The first link is the less direct one: in married couples, a warm and tender disposition (trait expressiveness) predicts both affectionate behavior and idealization of the partner (Miller et al., 2003).
text.formatted: The first link is the less direct one: in married couples, a warm and tender disposition (trait expressiveness) predicts both affectionate behavior and idealization of the partner <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Miller et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The second link is better documented.
Partners recognize the nonverbal display of love, and this display accompanies commitment-enhancing behavior (Gonzaga et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Partners recognize the nonverbal display of love, and this display accompanies commitment-enhancing behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gonzaga et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Declaring love communicates an intention to commit (Ackerman et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Declaring love communicates an intention to commit <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ackerman et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Acts that reveal love make rivals less interested in the actor (Gelbart et al., 2025), and relationships made visible on social media are perceived as more committed (Emery et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Acts that reveal love make rivals less interested in the actor <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gelbart et al., 2025)</ref>, and relationships made visible on social media are perceived as more committed <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Emery et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: To the extent that idealization feeds these expressions, it feeds signals of commitment.
Answers to an anonymous survey are not signals.

But dispositions shaped by their benefits of reciprocity and reputation do not switch off when no one is watching (for instance, people are generous in anonymous one-shot interactions; Delton et al., 2011; and they punish unfair behavior when their punishment cannot be seen; Jordan & Rand, 2020).
text.formatted: But dispositions shaped by their benefits of reciprocity and reputation do not switch off when no one is watching (for instance, people are generous in anonymous one-shot interactions; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Delton et al., 2011</ref>; and they punish unfair behavior when their punishment cannot be seen; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Jordan & Rand, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Anonymous answers can therefore reflect the motivation that produces signals, even though they are not signals themselves.
We therefore use the endorsement of idealizing statements as an indirect measure of the motivation behind romantic signaling, not as a measure of signaling itself.

If the value of signaling commitment declines with development, the endorsement of idealizing statements should decline too, relative to statements that describe the relationship without idealizing it.
Study 3 tests this implication.
It does not actually test whether respondents send fewer signals to their partners.
To test our hypothesis, we reanalyzed the cross-national dataset of Sorokowski and colleagues (2023), in which participants answered the 45 items of Sternberg's Triangular Love Scale.
text.formatted: To test our hypothesis, we reanalyzed the cross-national dataset of <ref type="bibr">Sorokowski and colleagues (2023)</ref>, in which participants answered the 45 items of Sternberg's Triangular Love Scale.

text.text: The items describe emotions, cognitions, and behaviors related to romantic relationships.
The analytic sample included 388,840 item-level responses from 8,792 participants in 45 countries (see Methods for exclusions).
Crucially for our purposes, these items vary widely in their degree of partner idealization.

Some items strongly imply idealization and exclusivity (e.g., "Nothing is more important to me than my relationship"), others involve moderate idealization (e.g., "I find my partner very personally attractive"), and still others involve no idealization at all (e.g., "I give considerable emotional support to my partner").
Rather than aggregating items into the traditional dimensions of passion, intimacy, and commitment, we treated partner idealization as a continuous item-level property.
This decision follows directly from the model.
Since the predicted decline reflects signaling rather than romantic experience as a whole, it should be detectable at the item level, where signaling content varies.
Four independent coders (three authors blind to the distribution of the data, one coder blind to the hypothesis) rated each of the 45 items for their level of partner idealization.
The reliability of the averaged rating was high (ICC(2,k) = 0.875).
Ratings were averaged to yield a single partner idealization score per item.
Before turning to the model, Figure 3A shows the pattern at the country level.
text.formatted: Before turning to the model, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref> shows the pattern at the country level.

text.text: We split the 45 items at the median partner idealization score (0.25) and computed, for each country, the mean endorsement of the 24 high-idealization items and of the 21 low-idealization items.
Endorsement of both groups of items is higher in moderately developed countries than in the least developed ones.

It levels off earlier, and falls further, for high-idealization items (e.g., "Nothing is more important to me than my relationship") than for low-idealization items (e.g., "I give considerable emotional support to my partner"): quadratic fits across countries peak at an HDI of 0.79 for high-idealization items and 0.86 for low-idealization items.
The gap between the two groups therefore widens with HDI (r = 0.58 across the 45 countries).

These country means describe the pattern but do not test it: they combine development with other differences between countries, and they depend on how respondents in each country use the rating scale.
The analyses below test the pattern on each participant's answers.
To test this pattern, we used the continuous variation in PI across all 45 items.

As pre-registered, we modeled each participant's response to each item (388,840 responses from 8,792 participants in 45 countries) as a function of the item's PI score, the HDI of the participant's country, the participant's SES, and their interactions, with random intercepts for participant, item, and country (model M0, pre-registered; see Methods for the full specification).
Following the preregistration, a prediction was supported if the 95% interval of a bootstrap excluded zero; because HDI varies between countries only, the bootstrap resampled countries.
The PI × HDI interaction combines a property of items with a property of countries.

We therefore also report a model that lets the effect of PI vary across countries and across participants (model M1, not preregistered; added during revision in response to a reviewer's suggestion), so that the interaction is tested against the variation between countries.
The key prediction is that the association between development and endorsement depends on how idealizing the item is.
This is captured by the PI × HDI interaction.

As predicted, this interaction was negative: the more an item implies partner idealization, the lower its endorsement in more developed countries, relative to the other items (M0: b = -0.048, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.061, -0.028]; M1: b = -0.050, 95% CI [-0.072, -0.027], t(42.4) = -4.43, p < .001).
text.formatted: As predicted, this interaction was negative: the more an item implies partner idealization, the lower its endorsement in more developed countries, relative to the other items (M0: b = -0.048, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.061, -0.028]; M1: b = -0.050, 95% CI [-0.072, -0.027], t(42.4) = -4.43, p < .001).

text.text: The pre-registered prediction for SES was not supported: the PI × SES interaction was negative, but its bootstrap interval included zero (M0: b = -0.007, 95% CI [-0.015, 0.001]).
In M1, which does not let this interaction vary between countries, it was significant (b = -0.010, 95% CI [-0.015, -0.005], t(8,741) = -4.14, p < .001).
text.formatted: In M1, which does not let this interaction vary between countries, it was significant (b = -0.010, 95% CI [-0.015, -0.005], t(8,741) = -4.14, p < .001).

text.text: This association was present within countries: participants who rated their economic situation higher than others in their country endorsed idealizing items relatively less (Supplementary Note 4).
Development was not associated with a uniform change in endorsement.

The quadratic term of HDI was negative (M0: b = -0.056, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.088, -0.015]), and it applies to all items: the pre-registered model has a single curvature, which the PI × HDI interaction shifts according to how idealizing the item is.
The implied slope of endorsement on HDI (in SD units) therefore crosses zero at a lower HDI for idealizing items.
In M1, for the most idealizing item, it is 0.19 at an HDI of 0.55, -0.02 at 0.75 and -0.24 (SE = 0.06) at 0.95, but for the least idealizing item, it is 0.37, 0.15 and -0.07 (SE = 0.05).
At the highest levels of development, endorsement thus declines for strongly idealizing items and does not change reliably for items without idealization.
The interaction of PI with squared HDI, added to M1, was close to zero (b = 0.002, p = .843).

text.text: The rise and fall of the country means of this survey may partly reflect differences in how respondents use rating scales rather than differences in love (Ulitzsch et al., 2024; for a reply, see Sorokowski & Kowal, 2024).

text.text: Such differences could also produce the PI × HDI interaction, even if they affected all items equally.
Extreme responding stretches answers away from the midpoint, which widens the distance between items, while the top of the scale compresses the answers to items already close to it, which narrows it.

The gap between idealizing and other items could therefore change with HDI if extreme responding differed between more and less developed countries, all the more so if idealizing items, often phrased in absolute terms, were the most sensitive to it.
We tested this in three ways (Supplementary Note 4).

First, across countries, extreme responding was not associated with HDI, whether measured by the share of answers at the top of the scale (r = 0.22, p = .146) or with a multi-process item response model (r = 0.16, p = .298; Böckenholt & Meiser, 2017).
